title: Tax-Deductible Donations Explained: How Charitable Deductions Work
excerpt: A plain guide to how US charitable deductions work for gifts to registered charities: IRS rules, limits and records. AbleHearts is not yet a registered charity, so gifts to AbleHearts are not currently tax-deductible.
author: AbleHearts Team
content:
## 💰 Understanding Tax-Deductible Donations When you give to a qualified (registered, tax-exempt) charity, the tax system in many countries lets you deduct some or all of that gift. Many donors don't fully understand how these deductions work. **Where AbleHearts stands:** AbleHearts is not yet a registered charity and does not have tax-exempt status, so gifts to AbleHearts are **not** tax-deductible today. Everything below describes how deductions work for gifts to organizations that *do* qualify, so you can plan your giving with clear eyes. This guide explains how US tax-deductible donations work, what the limits are, and what records the IRS expects. --- ## 📋 What Makes a Donation Tax-Deductible? ### ✅ Qualifying Requirements For your donation to be tax-deductible, it must meet these IRS criteria: 1. **Donate to a Qualified Organization** - 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization - Religious organizations (churches, temples, mosques) - Government entities for public purposes - Verified on IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search 2. **You Must Itemize Deductions** - Cannot claim if taking standard deduction - Standard deduction 2025: $14,600 (single), $29,200 (married) - Must have charitable + other deductions exceeding standard amount 3. **You Must Have Documentation** - Receipt for all donations - Bank statement or written acknowledgment for $250+ - Detailed records for non-cash donations ### ❌ What's NOT Tax-Deductible - Donations to individuals (even if they need help) - Political contributions - Donations to foreign charities (without US 501(c)(3) partnership) - Value of your time/service volunteering - Raffle tickets, bingo, lottery (entertainment portion) --- ## 💵 How Much Can You Deduct? ### Annual Deduction Limits (2025) The IRS limits how much you can deduct based on your **Adjusted Gross Income (AGI)**: #### Cash Donations: - **Up to 60% of AGI** to qualified public charities - **Up to 30% of AGI** to private foundations #### Non-Cash Donations: - **Up to 50% of AGI** for property (held >1 year) - **Up to 30% of AGI** for appreciated property ### 📊 Real Examples: **Example 1: Single Filer** - AGI: $80,000 - Maximum cash deduction: $48,000 (60% of $80,000) - You donate: $5,000 to a qualified US charity - ✅ Fully deductible **Example 2: Married Filing Jointly** - AGI: $150,000 - Maximum cash deduction: $90,000 (60% of $150,000) - You donate: $10,000 to a qualified US charity - ✅ Fully deductible **Example 3: High Earner** - AGI: $500,000 - Maximum cash deduction: $300,000 (60% of $500,000) - You donate: $50,000 to a qualified US charity - ✅ Fully deductible --- ## 🧮 Calculate Your Tax Savings ### How Tax Deductions Save You Money **Tax deductions reduce your taxable income**, which means you pay less in taxes. The amount you save depends on your **tax bracket**. ### 2025 Federal Tax Brackets:
| Tax Bracket | Single Income | Married Income | Tax on $1,000 Donation | |-------------|---------------|----------------|------------------------| | 10% | $0 - $11,600 | $0 - $23,200 | $100 savings | | 12% | $11,601 - $47,150 | $23,201 - $94,300 | $120 savings | | 22% | $47,151 - $100,525 | $94,301 - $201,050 | $220 savings | | 24% | $100,526 - $191,950 | $201,051 - $383,900 | $240 savings | | 32% | $191,951 - $243,725 | $383,901 - $487,450 | $320 savings | | 35% | $243,726 - $609,350 | $487,451 - $731,200 | $350 savings | | 37% | $609,351+ | $731,201+ | $370 savings |
### 💡 Quick Calculation Formula: **Tax Savings = Donation Amount × Your Tax Bracket** **Example Calculations:** **Scenario 1: $500 Donation, 22% Tax Bracket** - Tax savings: $500 × 0.22 = **$110** - Net cost after tax savings: $500 - $110 = **$390** **Scenario 2: $2,000 Donation, 32% Tax Bracket** - Tax savings: $2,000 × 0.32 = **$640** - Net cost: $2,000 - $640 = **$1,360** **Scenario 3: $10,000 Donation, 37% Tax Bracket** - Tax savings: $10,000 × 0.37 = **$3,700** - Net cost: $10,000 - $3,700 = **$6,300** --- ## 📝 Documentation Requirements ### What You Need to Keep The IRS has specific documentation requirements based on donation amount: #### Donations Under $250: - Bank statement showing: - Name of charity - Date of donation - Amount donated - OR receipt from charity #### Donations $250 - $500: - Written acknowledgment from charity stating: - Amount of cash donation - Description of non-cash donation - Statement that no goods/services were provided - OR description and value of goods/services if provided #### Donations $501 - $5,000: - All documentation from $250+ category - PLUS your own records showing: - How you acquired the property - Date of acquisition - Cost or other basis - Fair market value determination method #### Donations Over $5,000: - All documentation from $501+ category - PLUS qualified appraisal for non-cash items - Form 8283 (Noncash Charitable Contributions) ### 🚨 Common Documentation Mistakes: ❌ **"I donated cash at church, but I don't have a receipt"** - Solution: Always get a receipt or use check/credit card for records ❌ **"I donated $500, but I only have an email confirmation"** - Solution: That's fine! Email counts as written acknowledgment ❌ **"I donated clothes worth $1,000, but I didn't get an appraisal"** - Solution: For $1,000, appraisal not needed. Keep receipt + list of items --- ## 🎯 Strategies to Maximize Your Deduction ### 1. Bunch Your Donations 📦 **The Problem:** Your annual donations don't exceed the standard deduction. **The Solution:** "Bunch" 2-3 years of donations into one year. **Example:** - Standard deduction: $14,600 (single) - Normal giving: $5,000/year **Without Bunching (3 years):** - Year 1: Donate $5,000, take standard deduction ($14,600) - Year 2: Donate $5,000, take standard deduction ($14,600) - Year 3: Donate $5,000, take standard deduction ($14,600) - Total deductions: $43,800 (standard × 3) - Total given: $15,000 **With Bunching (3 years):** - Year 1: Donate $15,000, itemize ($15,000 + $2,000 other = $17,000) - Year 2: Donate $0, take standard deduction ($14,600) - Year 3: Donate $0, take standard deduction ($14,600) - Total deductions: $46,200 (itemize + standard × 2) - Total given: $15,000 - **Extra tax savings: $2,400 × your tax rate** ### 2. Donate Appreciated Stock 📈 **Why It's Powerful:** - Avoid capital gains tax on appreciation - Deduct full market value - Double tax benefit! **Example:** You bought stock for $1,000, now worth $5,000. **If You Sell Stock Then Donate Cash:** - Capital gains tax: $4,000 × 15% = **$600 tax paid** - Donate $4,400 after-tax proceeds - Deduction: $4,400 **If You Donate Stock Directly:** - Capital gains tax: **$0** (avoided entirely) - Donate full $5,000 worth - Deduction: $5,000 - **You saved $600 + helped more!** ### 3. Use a Donor-Advised Fund (DAF) 🏦 **What It Is:** A charitable investment account. **How It Works:** 1. Donate money/stock to DAF (get immediate tax deduction) 2. Funds grow tax-free in the account 3. Recommend grants to qualified charities over time **Benefits:** - Take deduction this year, give later - Simplify recordkeeping (1 receipt vs. many) - Donate anonymously if desired - Grow your charitable impact tax-free ### 4. Make a Qualified Charitable Distribution (QCD) 👴 **Who Can Use This:** Age 70½ or older with an IRA **How It Works:** - Transfer up to $105,000 (2025 limit) from your IRA directly to charity - Counts toward your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) - **NOT included in your taxable income** (even better than a deduction!) **Example:** - Age 72, RMD required: $15,000 - Transfer $15,000 from IRA to a qualified charity as a QCD - You satisfy RMD requirement - $15,000 never appears as income - You save: $15,000 × your tax rate ### 5. Time Your Donations Strategically 📅 **End-of-Year Giving:** - Donate by December 31 to claim deduction for that year - Credit card donations count when charged (even if paid later) - Check/cash must be delivered by Dec 31 **High-Income Year:** - Got a bonus? Donate more this year to offset higher income - Sold property at a gain? Donate to reduce taxable income --- ## 🧾 How to Claim Your Deduction (Step-by-Step) ### Step 1: Gather Your Documentation - Collect all donation receipts - Organize by charity and date - Total your contributions ### Step 2: Determine If You Should Itemize - Add up all itemized deductions: - Charitable contributions - State/local taxes (capped at $10,000) - Mortgage interest - Medical expenses exceeding 7.5% of AGI - If total > standard deduction → itemize - If total < standard deduction → take standard ### Step 3: Complete IRS Forms - **Schedule A (Form 1040):** Report itemized deductions - **Line 11:** Cash contributions - **Line 12:** Non-cash contributions - **Form 8283:** If non-cash donations > $500 ### Step 4: Keep Records for 3+ Years - IRS can audit within 3 years - Keep donation receipts, bank statements - Store electronically for easy access --- ## ❓ FAQs: Tax-Deductible Donations ### Q: Can I deduct donations if I take the standard deduction? **A:** No. You must itemize deductions to claim charitable contributions. However, there was a special provision during COVID that expired in 2021. ### Q: I donated $500 but charity only sent a $400 receipt. What do I do? **A:** Only deduct the $400 with proper documentation. Contact charity to correct the receipt if it's an error. ### Q: Can I deduct donations to Mary & Lydia, or to AbleHearts? **A:** No. Donations to individuals aren't tax-deductible, and AbleHearts is not yet a registered charity or a qualified 501(c)(3) organization, so gifts to AbleHearts aren't tax-deductible either. We will update this post once our registration is complete. ### Q: What if my donation is over the AGI limit? **A:** You can carry forward the excess for up to 5 years. For example, if your AGI is $100,000 and you donate $70,000, you can deduct $60,000 this year and $10,000 next year. ### Q: Do I need an appraisal for donated items? **A:** Only for non-cash items valued over $5,000. For example, donating a car worth $6,000 requires an appraisal. ### Q: Can I deduct the value of my volunteer time? **A:** No. However, you CAN deduct unreimbursed expenses related to volunteering (e.g., mileage at 14¢/mile, supplies purchased). ### Q: What if I get something in return for my donation? **A:** You can only deduct the amount that exceeds the fair market value of what you received. For example, if you pay $100 for a charity dinner worth $40, you can deduct $60. --- ## 💡 Where AbleHearts Stands ### Honest status - **Not yet a registered charity.** AbleHearts is a small grassroots effort for Mary and Lydia, and the registration paperwork is still in progress. - **No tax-exempt status.** We are not a 501(c)(3), a CRA-registered charity or a Kenyan exempt organization. - **Not tax-deductible.** Gifts to AbleHearts cannot be claimed as a charitable deduction today, in the US or anywhere else. - **A record, not a tax receipt.** We are glad to send a record of your gift for your own files, but it is not an official tax receipt. ### What you can count on - **Several ways to give:** card or Apple Pay via Paystack, M-PESA, bank transfer and cryptocurrency - **Transparency:** receipts, photos and updates on the Transparency page and the blog, so you can see what your gift did - **Direct contact:** you can talk to the family on WhatsApp or through the Contact page --- ## 🚀 Before You Give If a tax deduction matters to you this year, use the steps above with a registered charity and keep good records. If you would like to help Mary & Lydia directly, knowing the gift is not tax-deductible, you can [donate securely](/donate). Every gift goes to their needs. --- *Disclaimer: This guide is for informational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Consult with a qualified tax professional for your specific situation. Tax laws and limits are subject to change.*
